description.en:
A beautiful topic-wise e-book on the art and culture of Assam — dance and music traditions, Ankiya Naat and Bhaona, handloom and silk, masks and paintings, the Sattras of Sankardeva, monuments and the colourful festivals of the land.

This is an online reading e-book only. It cannot be downloaded as a PDF.
description.as:
অসমৰ কলা-সংস্কৃতিৰ বিষয়ে এটা সুন্দৰ বিষয়-ভিত্তিক ই-বুক — নৃত্য আৰু সংগীত পৰম্পৰা, অংকীয়া নাট আৰু ভাওনা, হস্ততন্তু আৰু ৰেচম, মুখা আৰু চিত্ৰকলা, শংকৰদেৱৰ সত্ৰ, স্মৃতিসৌধ আৰু ৰঙীন উৎসৱসমূহ।

এই ই-বুক কেৱল অনলাইন পঠনৰ বাবে। ইয়াক PDF হিচাপে ডাউনলোড কৰিব নোৱাৰি।

content.en:
Sattriya dance is the classical dance form of Assam, introduced by the great saint-reformer Srimanta Sankardeva in the 15th century. It was performed inside the Sattras (Vaishnavite monasteries) and was recognised as a classical dance of India in 2000. The male dancers of the Sattras are called Sattriya dancers, and the tradition includes both solo and group performances.

Assam also has a rich tradition of folk dances and music. The Bihu dance, performed during the Bohag Bihu festival, is the most popular folk dance and is accompanied by songs of love and spring. Other folk dances include the Bhortal Nritya (with cymbals), Jhumur of the tea tribes, Deodhani, and the Ojapali form which blends music, dance and storytelling.

Ojapali is one of the oldest performing arts of Assam and is divided mainly into three styles — Suknanni (mythological tales), Maroi (worship of the snake goddess Manasa) and Bejali. Popular folk instruments of Assam include the dhol, pepa (made of buffalo horn), gogona, toka, and the Kham, a long drum used by the Ahoms.

Srimanta Sankardeva (1449–1568) was the greatest cultural figure of Assam. Through the Neo-Vaishnavite movement he preached devotion to Lord Krishna and used art as a medium of worship. His literary works include the Kirtan Ghosha and the dramas known as Ankiya Naat, while his disciple Madhavdeva composed the famous Namghosha.

The Sattras, established by Sankardeva and his followers, are religious-cum-cultural institutions that preserved dance, drama, music and painting for centuries. The Namghar (prayer hall) is the centre of community worship in Assamese villages.

Bhaona is the traditional one-act theatrical performance based on the Ankiya Naat plays of Sankardeva. Performers wear colourful costumes and masks, and the presentation is accompanied by the khol (drum) and taal (cymbals). The mask-making tradition of Samaguri in Majuli district has earned national fame, and Majuli itself is the largest river island in the world and the heart of the Sattriya culture.

Assam is famous for its handloom and silk. The three main varieties of silk produced are Muga (golden yellow, found only in Assam), Pat and Eri. The traditional Assamese dress — the Mekhela Chador and the Gamosa — is woven on handlooms in almost every household. The Gamosa, a white cloth with red borders, is a symbol of Assamese identity and is also used in the Bihu dance.

Assam is called the land of festivals. The most important is Bihu, celebrated three times a year — Bohag (Rongali) Bihu in April, Kati (Kongali) Bihu in autumn and Magh (Bhogali) Bihu in January. Other festivals include Ambubachi Mela at Kamakhya, the Ali-Ai-Ligang of the Mishing tribe, Baishagu of the Bodo people and Rongker of the Karbis.

Famous monuments and heritage sites of Assam include the Kamakhya Temple on the Nilachal hill, the Sivasagar monuments — the Rang Ghar, Talatal Ghar and the Shiva Dol — built by the Ahom kings, the Charaideo Maidams (royal burial mounds of the Ahoms), the Umananda Temple on the Peacock Island in the Brahmaputra, and the Kaziranga and Manas national parks which reflect the natural heritage of the state.
